## Stage 0 — Document Accessibility Report The supplied main document contains extracted text for physical PDF pages 1–20. All 20 pages can therefore be assessed textually. Seventeen page images are supplied: pp. 1, 2, 5–16, and 18–20. These images were directly inspected; pp. 3, 4, and 17 have text-only coverage. The supplied accessibility metadata reports native text on every page, no low-text pages, and no embedded supplementary files. This report does not independently verify the PDF file or its hash; the supplied source identifier is retained as provenance. The available sequence reaches the conclusion, references, and Appendices A–E, with no apparent gap in the extracted page sequence. That supports coverage of this supplied 20-page version, but does not establish that every associated artifact or publication supplement is present. Figures 1–9 and Tables 1–15 are available on rendered pages. Their principal structures and values are readable. Figure 3 has dense small labels, so its 160 individual agent-by-website bar segments are not all independently transcribed. Figure 6 has extraction artifacts and stray text in its extracted representation; interpretation follows the visible diagram and surrounding method description rather than treating those artifacts as substantive content. Equations are sparse: the recall fraction is readable, while some diagram notation is less reliable. Appendices A–E are included. Appendix C provides experimental platforms and prompts, not an executable implementation. The project website, cited repositories, actual benchmark snapshots, annotation records, restoration code, defense-generation prompts, and experimental logs are not supplied or inspected. No browsing, tools, external verification, or OCR was used. Native text was compared with supplied visuals where possible; remaining discrepancies are reported below. Evidence labels throughout: **[A] author-reported**, **[B] directly observable**, **[C] analyst-derived**, and **[D] analyst interpretation**. No external information [E] is introduced. HIGH confidence means clear supplied support, not independent replication. MEDIUM means support exists but reporting or interpretation limits precision. LOW means a material uncertainty remains. UNKNOWN means the supplied work cannot answer the point. ## 1. Plain-Language Orientation WebCloak studies how large language model (LLM) technology can help people collect website content automatically, especially image URLs. A URL is an address from which a resource can be retrieved. The paper treats a malicious user operating an AI scraper as the attacker and the website owner as the defender. This differs from studying a legitimate assistant tricked by a malicious website: here, the assistant is deliberately being used to scrape a benign site. [A; pp. 1–4] The researchers built LLMCrawlBench from 237 offline webpage snapshots, drawn from 50 high-traffic websites across five categories, with 10,895 annotated image assets. They first evaluated 32 scraper variants and then examined three leading representatives in more detail: Gemini-2.5-pro generating scraping scripts, Crawl4AI integrating LLMs into extraction, and Browser-Use controlling a browser. Their central architectural observation is that agents usually cannot economically process an entire large webpage directly. Instead, software first parses and reduces its structure; the LLM then interprets the reduced content. [A; pp. 2, 5–7] WebCloak attacks both dependencies. Its structural layer changes image tags, attribute names, and resource representations, while JavaScript restores their visible appearance for people. Its semantic layer places hidden, optimized text around assets to confuse extraction-oriented LLM interpretation. In the ordinary tested configurations, the paper reports zero image-scraping recall with the full defense. Under some adaptive conditions, however, small nonzero recall remains. The headline reduction from 88.7% to 0% refers to a selected high-vulnerability comparison subset; other whole-benchmark baselines are reported separately and inconsistently. [A; pp. 8–12] The central contribution is a combined benchmark, measurement study, and website-owner defense. It is not a direct experiment comparing standalone LLM security with web-agent security. For the requested research question, its relevance is **analyst inference**: connecting a model to webpage parsing and browser workflows adds structural dependencies and channels through which untrusted page content can influence behavior. The paper demonstrates those dependencies in scraping systems, but does not establish how much more vulnerable an agent is than the same model used alone. [D; pp. 3–4, 7–9] ## 2. Document Roadmap **Document identity.** The original title is *WebCloak: Characterizing and Mitigating Threats from LLM-Driven Web Agents as Intelligent Scrapers*. Authors are Xinfeng Li, Tianze Qiu, Yingbin Jin, Lixu Wang, Hanqing Guo, Xiaojun Jia, XiaoFeng Wang, and Wei Dong. The title page lists Nanyang Technological University, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, and University of Hawaii at Manoa; Wei Dong is marked corresponding author. Appendix D identifies a meta-review for the 2026 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy. This is supplied publication-process information, not externally verified publication status. Three artifact badges appear on p. 1: available, functional, and reproduced. Their presence does not substitute for inspecting those artifacts. [A/B] **Type.** This is a mixed cybersecurity, computer-systems, empirical measurement, and benchmark paper. It includes a defense-generation procedure and two user studies. It is neither a systematic literature review nor a theoretical proof paper. **Inventory.** S1 Introduction and abstract, pp. 1–3; S2 Background and Related Work, §§2.1–2.3, pp. 3–4; S3 Threat Model, §§3.1–3.3, p. 4; S4 LLMCrawlBench Construction, p. 5; S5 Large-Scale LLM Crawler Measurement, §§5.1–5.3, pp. 5–8; S6 WebCloak: Dual-Layer Protection, §§6.1–6.3, pp. 8–9; S7 Evaluation, §§7.1–7.5, pp. 9–13; S8 Discussion, including limitations and ethical practices, pp. 13–14; S9 Conclusion, p. 14. Acknowledgments and 67 references occupy pp. 14–16. Appendix A has A.1 website curation, A.2 snapshot preprocessing, and A.3 image annotation. Appendix B describes measurement supplementary details and points to a standardized script-generation prompt. Appendix C contains C.1 platforms, C.2 task prompts, C.3 adaptive-adversary prompts, C.4 audio/text generalization, and C.5 usability study. Appendix D includes D.1 summary, D.2 contributions, D.3 acceptance reasons, and D.4 concerns. Appendix E responds to those concerns. Figures F1–F9 and Tables T1–T15 retain original numbering below. E1 identifies the recall fraction on p. 10. ALG1 identifies the described iterative semantic-defense procedure, which is prose rather than numbered pseudocode. No theorem, lemma, formal hypothesis, or keyword list is supplied. The logical sequence is: characterize misuse → build a repeatable testbed → identify operational dependencies → construct a two-layer defense → test extraction, adaptation, usability, and cost → discuss boundaries. Appendix D supplies independent review concerns within the document, and Appendix E supplies the authors' response; both materially qualify the novelty and effectiveness discussion. ## 3. Background and Context **Web scraping** means automatically extracting website content. The paper distinguishes simple Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) requests with parsing libraries from browser automation capable of executing JavaScript. Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) describes webpage elements; the Document Object Model (DOM) is their structured representation used by browser and automation software. Tags such as `` identify images, while `src` and `srcset` identify image resources or alternatives. Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) control presentation. [A; pp. 3, 8, 16] Three paradigms matter. **LLM-to-Script (L2S)** uses natural-language requests to generate code, usually Python; that code performs scraping and may require correction. **LLM-Native Crawlers (LNCs)** integrate LLMs into extraction pipelines and commonly use simplified HTML. **LLM-based Web Agents (LWAs)** operate browsers using DOM or accessibility information, screenshots, or both. LWA is a category, not a guarantee that every tested agent sees the same inputs. [A; p. 3] A **context window** limits how much model input can be processed at once. The paper reports average raw HTML length of 332,079 tokens and cites example limits of 128k and 200k tokens. Those are author-provided contextual comparisons; they were not checked against current product specifications. **Markdown conversion** turns HTML into a shorter textual format. **Parse-then-interpret** names the dependency between non-LLM structural preprocessing and subsequent LLM semantic processing. L2S differs: it commonly generates a parser from general web knowledge instead of itself reading the whole page. [A; pp. 2, 7] **Prompt injection** in this paper is page-carried text that attempts to redirect the model away from the user's extraction objective. WebCloak uses it defensively. The same text is untrusted evidence for this analysis: none of the supplied example instructions were followed. **Polymorphic** structural protection means the representation changes between sessions. A **cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator (CSPRNG)** produces randomized structural identifiers. **Shadow DOM** is the named restoration mechanism in which the authors say recovered URLs are stored with reduced visibility to agent automation. No browser-level impossibility guarantee is proved. [A; pp. 8–9] ## 4. Research Problem and Gap **Existing problem.** Valuable public-facing content can be harvested without the owner's authorization. The authors emphasize images, intellectual-property concerns, unauthorized aggregation, and the ability of natural-language-controlled tools to lower the technical barrier. Their examples of real-world abuse are literature/background claims, not incidents experimentally investigated here. [A; pp. 1, 3] **Shortcomings of prior approaches, according to the authors.** Traditional scripts require site-specific maintenance. Internet Protocol (IP) and User-Agent checks can be spoofed; CAPTCHAs face multimodal-model challenges; behavioral analysis has per-request costs. Static code obfuscation can fail once a browser renders a readable DOM. Existing agent benchmarks emphasize benign task success and generally lack image-scraping ground truth. Prior agent-security studies mostly consider the agent as victim rather than as an attacker-operated scraper. [A; pp. 1, 3–5] **Research gap.** The paper seeks systematic measurement across scraper paradigms and a defense grounded in their common operational mechanisms. Its claim to be the first such systematic characterization is an author novelty claim; the supplied paper alone cannot verify priority across all literature. [A; pp. 2, 4] **Motivation and scope.** The intended intervention is lightweight protection inside the page rather than expensive centralized detection. The target is scalable misuse by novice-to-intermediate operators, not every possible extraction method or expert attacker. The defender should retain the human-visible content. This creates a deliberate asymmetry: humans are intended to see the same page while automated structural and semantic extraction becomes harder. [A; p. 4] ## 5. Research Questions / Objectives / Hypotheses The introduction states three questions: **RQ1:** how feasible current LLM-driven agents are for illicit extraction from real-world websites; **RQ2:** their underlying mechanisms, failure modes, and exploitable dependencies; **RQ3:** how owners can defend effectively, robustly, and lightly while preserving user experience. These are answered by the measurement, mechanism analysis, and defense evaluation respectively. [A; p. 1] Section 7 reuses question labels differently: §7.2 is RQ1 effectiveness, §7.3 RQ2 robustness, §7.4 RQ3 usability, and §7.5 RQ4 overhead. These are evaluation dimensions, not the same numbering as the introductory questions. Both systems are preserved rather than silently merged. [A; pp. 10–13] Explicit objectives include comparing 32 variants, selecting representative strong scrapers, quantifying effort and resource costs, constructing an image-specific reproducible benchmark, and assessing a dual-layer defense against adaptation and across environments. No formal null or alternative hypotheses, preregistered decision rules, or significance thresholds are specified. The requested question about agents versus standalone LLMs is an external analytical framing supplied by the user, not an experimental question tested by this paper. ## 6. Assumptions / Threat Model The **attacker** is a malicious operator seeking automated, unauthorized extraction of images, audio, or text with little manual effort and low cost. The attacker can use L2S, LNC, or LWA systems, configure prompts, inspect source and DOM, and understand HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Knowledge-guided adaptation may provide a protected page and restoration script to an LLM for reverse engineering. [A; §3, p. 4] The assumed operator is novice-to-intermediate and prioritizes scale. The model excludes sustained expensive per-session manual code repair, modification of core closed-source agent logic, and intensive per-site jailbreak optimization. Highly resourced bespoke attackers fall outside the intended protection claim. Thus low measured recall does not imply that resources are cryptographically inaccessible or that all methods of copying a human-visible asset have been eliminated. The latter is an analyst interpretation of the stated scope. [A/D] The **defender** controls the webpage representation and can insert transformations, restoration JavaScript, and optimized semantic cues. Legitimate users are expected to execute JavaScript. The defense aims for visual transparency, extraction reduction, adaptive robustness, and practical integration. The page's appearance is trusted for usability purposes; its hidden text is deliberately adversarial to scraper interpretation. The supplied design does not formalize a comprehensive trusted-computing base or access-control proof. [A; pp. 4, 8–9] An important scope distinction is that the experiments run on local snapshots, despite frequent wording about threats to live websites. The live-web origin supplies realistic content and layout, but local execution does not directly test continuous production behavior, authenticated interactions, or changing server responses. [A/D; pp. 5, 14, 16] ## 7. Methodology ### Benchmark and annotation LLMCrawlBench contains 237 distinct pages from 50 sites in marketplaces, lifestyle, design, travel, and entertainment. Selection favors high traffic, complex layouts, and dense valuable visual assets. The authors report 10,895 unique image assets and mean HTML length 332,079 tokens. There is no model-training dataset or train/validation/test split described: this is an evaluation benchmark. [A; pp. 5, 16] To freeze changing content, the authors saved offline HTML and local assets. They neutralized nonessential or problematic scripts, localized CSS/fonts/images, rewrote resource paths, and simplified responsive `srcset` to a high-resolution local `src`. Each page was compared visually with a timestamped screenshot of the live counterpart. The purpose was repeatable rendering with minimal necessary intervention. The supplied work does not quantify fidelity verification error or provide the screenshots used for all 237 comparisons. [A; Appendix A.2] Candidate images came from `` tags and CSS `background-image` properties. Filters removed images smaller than 64×64 pixels, filenames containing logo/icon/avatar/spinner indicators, and non-content locations such as navigation, headers, and footers. Trained annotators then selected semantically relevant main-content images. Annotator count, agreement statistics, adjudication rules, and a per-category page allocation are not supplied. The benchmark target is therefore main-content extraction, which is narrower than literally every visible image. [A/D; Appendix A.3] ### Scraper measurement Phase 1 tests 19 L2S models, five LNC tools, and eight LWAs on five pages, one per category. Phase 2 tests Gemini-2.5-pro, Crawl4AI, and Browser-Use on all 237 pages. Default requests ask for image URLs. Appendix C includes more specific requests and an L2S prompt that asks for Python code, URL JSON output, downloads, and an image count, while suggesting browser automation for dynamic content. These are reported experimental inputs, not instructions for this analysis. [A; pp. 6–7, 17] The expert/novice comparison uses five experts and five novices. Experts manually implement scraping; novices use the three representative tools. Perceived difficulty and manual effort use five-point scales. The usability study is separate: 35 participants inspect randomized pairs of original/protected versions of five pages and answer five questions on a seven-point scale. Participant selection, demographic distributions, and formal statistical tests are not reported. [A; pp. 6–7, 18] ### Structural protection Part 1 first normalizes nonstandard source attributes, then changes structural representations per session. Random attributes replace conventional resource cues; image tags may become `
` elements; encoded or encrypted resource values and honeypot `src` values may be inserted. A separate JavaScript snippet restores the display after DOM loading. The authors describe preserving obfuscated attributes and storing recovered URLs in Shadow DOM, with CSS-background presentation mentioned as an alternative to direct image `src` representation. [A; pp. 2, 8] The paper calls critical URLs encrypted but does not specify a cryptographic algorithm, key handling, or a formal secrecy property. The experimentally supported goal is confusing the tested parsing pipelines while retaining display, not proving resource confidentiality against arbitrary client instrumentation. [A/D] ### Semantic protection: ALG1 Part 2 identifies three zones per target image: **pre**, hidden text before it; **intra**, its `alt` attribute; and **post**, hidden text after it. Random tags and CSS styles hide added elements from people. Content strategies include misleading asset descriptions, safety/policy warnings, and attention diversion or honeypots. The authors optimize these cues to survive the simplified representation consumed by agents. [A; p. 9] A Defend LLM, exemplified by GPT-4o-mini, generates candidate triples of snippets for a small template group. An Attack LLM, exemplified by GPT-4o, attempts extraction from simplified minimal HTML containing those targets. Candidate protection rates are scored; top-performing strategies are refined, including combinations of effective ideas. Iteration stops at a maximum depth or when enough variants perfectly block targets. The winning template is adapted to other images and inserted into the full page. `branchfactor`, `top_k`, depth, and success-count stopping parameters are named but their numerical settings are not supplied. [A] Construction order matters: semantic optimization and insertion occur first on the original page context; structural obfuscation follows. Figure 4's conceptual pairing should not be read as overriding this explicit implementation sequence. [A; §6.3] ### Platforms, comparisons, and reporting Default execution uses Ubuntu 22.04, Intel Xeon Gold at 2.8 GHz, 128 GB RAM, and Chrome. Additional platforms are macOS 14.1 on a MacBook M1 Pro with 16 GB RAM and Windows 11 on AMD Ryzen 7 7735HS with 16 GB RAM. Browser robustness includes Chrome, Firefox, Brave, Edge, and Safari. Exact tool releases, browser versions, API snapshots, decoding settings, random seeds, run counts, and confidence intervals are not specified. [A; pp. 6, 16] Baselines are original snapshots, full-code obfuscation, dynamic JavaScript loading, static target-tag replacement, and naive unoptimized semantic interference. Original snapshots retain existing site complexity and anti-scraping measures. Metrics include recall, precision, minimal viable recall, execution time, token consumption, CPU/memory percentages, Lighthouse loading measures, visual similarity, and subjective ratings. Reporting inconsistencies in definitions and aggregates are retained in Sections 13–14. ## 8. Experiments / Analyses **X1 — Broad feasibility, introductory RQ1.** Thirty-two variants operate on five category-representative pages. Table 1 and Figure 3 assess operational status and extraction. The authors report 84.4% can extract multiple correct images, while 30 of 32 are runnable. Top-performing recall entries are 84.2% L2S, 98.0% LNC, and 99.3% LWA. Minimal viable recall is separately 73.7%, 76.0%, and 25.0%. Five pages are a screening sample, not the full benchmark. [A; p. 6] **X2 — Expert/novice effort.** Five experts and five novices compare manual development with tool assistance. Manual coding takes 31:31, Gemini L2S 01:27 or 04:01 on dynamic pages, Crawl4AI 02:03, and Browser-Use 04:09. Experts report difficulty 4.8, reduced to 3.2 when LLM queries are allowed; novice difficulty is 2.3, 1.3, and 1.5. The small study supports lower reported effort; exact comparative extraction-success scores are not included in Table 2. [A; pp. 6–7] **X3 — Full-benchmark scraper profiles, RQ1/RQ2.** Three selected agents run across 237 pages. Table 4 gives recall/precision of 65.0/78.5 for Gemini, 71.0/81.7 for Crawl4AI, and 60.4/88.8 for Browser-Use. Token overhead is 9,998, 32,518, and 15,053. Table 3 gives category variation. Strong representatives demonstrate feasibility but are not an unbiased estimate of every available agent. [A/D; p. 7] **X4 — Mechanism analysis, introductory RQ2.** Figures 1 and 9 and §5.3 connect large HTML inputs with simplification and code-generated parsing. The authors identify predictable structural representations and LLM interpretation as distinct intervention points. The supplied work describes this as empirical investigation but does not present instrumented traces or a formal frequency count for every pipeline. [A/D; pp. 2, 7–8, 19] **X5 — Full-benchmark defense, evaluation effectiveness.** §7.2 reports initial recall 57.5%, 62.5%, and 54.4%, then 0.0% for all three with WebCloak. Those baseline values differ from Table 4's whole-benchmark scraper characterization. No explanation or separate whole-benchmark result table resolves the difference. [A; p. 10] **X6 — Defense-baseline comparison.** Twenty-seven deliberately difficult pages from Walmart, Allrecipes, Behance, Booking.com, and Eventbrite are selected for high baseline recall. Table 5 compares four alternatives with WebCloak. The latter has zero recall and precision for all agents; original recall is 93.1%, 95.3%, and 77.7%. The selected sample explains the headline 88.7% average and should not be equated with the entire benchmark. [A; pp. 10–11] **X7 — Instruction variation.** Default, targeted, conditional, and adversarial extraction requests yield varying unprotected performance in Table 6, but all reported protected recall/precision entries are zero. Exact sample allocation per prompt type is not restated. Targeted descriptions differ between the generic main-product-image example and the recipe-image template; these are distinct reported examples. [A; pp. 11, 17] **X8 — Audio/text generalization.** Ten supplementary evaluation pages comprise five music pages and five news pages. Audio extraction targets `.mp3` URLs; text tasks target content snippets, with the supplied template requesting paragraphs containing specified text. Table 7 reports all protected values as zero. Its text aggregate and the adjacent description conflict with per-agent values, limiting confidence in the aggregate. [A; pp. 11, 18] **X9 — Backend switching.** Crawl4AI is evaluated with four LLM backends. Table 8 reports zero protected recall throughout. Nearby prose reports a DeepSeek-V3 outlier producing 2.9% recall. The disagreement is unresolved. This experiment supports broad backend coverage, but not an unequivocal all-backends-zero conclusion. [A; p. 11] **X10 — Part 1 adaptation.** Static target replacement is compared with dynamic structural obfuscation under naive and adaptive attempts. L2S recall rises from 0 to 52.3% for the static baseline, versus 0 to 0.13% for Part 1. Crawl4AI rises to 2.7% versus 0.22%; Browser-Use remains zero in both. These are layer-isolation results, not the full-defense ordinary configuration. [A; pp. 11–12] **X11 — Part 2 removal.** Crawl4AI and Browser-Use operate against the semantic layer alone while increasing proportions of its cues are removed. At 90% removal, recall is 30.5% and 21.2%; Figure 7 shows substantial recovery at complete removal. L2S is excluded because the layer primarily targets interpretation-oriented agents. The prose incorrectly refers to isolating Part 1's resilience although the stated setup isolates Part 2. [A/B; p. 12] **X12 — Full-defense adaptive adversaries.** Refined, knowledgeable, and multi-turn knowledgeable attacks test increasing information and refinement. Table 10 gives refined recall 0/0.22/0; knowledgeable 0.20/1.58/0; and multi-turn L2S 0.30%. The latter is not applicable to the tested sessionless Crawl4AI/Browser-Use configurations. This evaluates two to three refinement turns, not unrestricted adaptation. [A; pp. 12, 17–18] **X13 — Environment robustness.** Browser-Use with WebCloak has reported recall 0.0% across five macOS browsers and Chrome on Windows/Ubuntu. No per-environment detailed result table is supplied. [A; p. 12] **X14 — Human usability.** Five randomly selected pages are assessed with loading metrics, visual similarity, and 35 participants. Ratings are 1.42–1.77 on the seven-point negative-impact scale; Figure 8 gives disagreement rates 89.1–99.4%. No uncertainty or significance tests accompany these values. Loading prose conflicts with Table 11. [A/B; pp. 13, 18–19] **X15 — Overhead and dynamic-content simulation.** Tables 14–15 assess size/tokens and generation/restoration time. Average file-size increase is reported as 20.8%, token increase 6.4%, server generation 179.7 s, and client restoration 0.052 s. Part 1 alone averages 13.0 ms/page; Part 2 dominates generation. A preliminary content-update simulation is described favorably without sample size, update regime, or numerical outcomes. [A; pp. 13, 19] ## 9. Results The strongest supported findings are conditional. First, many tested tools can extract assets with simple requests, but operational maturity varies: ScrapeGraphAI has JSON parsing failures, Proxy Lite returns hallucinatory URLs, SeeAct omits source attributes, and UI-only tools struggle with multi-step saving. These are observed author-reported failures in tested configurations, not inherent impossibility results. [A; p. 6] Second, extraction quality differs: Crawl4AI leads Table 4 recall at 71.0%; Browser-Use leads precision at 88.8%; Gemini script generation is comparatively flexible but may require debugging or Selenium. Category dependence is substantial: Crawl4AI marketplace recall is 45.4%, versus lifestyle 82.5%; Browser-Use travel precision is 99.8%. A single mean hides those differences. [A; p. 7] Third, ordinary full-defense evaluations report zero recall, whereas full-defense knowledgeable adaptation produces up to 1.58% for Crawl4AI in Table 10. The conclusion should therefore be 'zero in the reported ordinary conditions and very low in the modeled adaptive conditions,' rather than universal prevention. [A/D; pp. 10–12] Fourth, static structural defenses can look strong before adaptation. Table 5's static replacement already blocks Crawl4AI and Browser-Use in the initial condition. The added value of dynamic protection is clearer in the adaptive comparisons and its L2S protection, not merely in an initial all-agents average. [A/D; pp. 10–12] **Derived numerical distinction.** Table 5 original recalls average to (93.1 + 95.3 + 77.7)/3 = 88.7%. Moving from that average to zero is an 88.7-percentage-point reduction, or a 100% relative reduction within that specific experiment. It is not an 88.7% relative reduction. Table 4's recalls average to (65.0 + 71.0 + 60.4)/3 = 65.4667%, while §7.2's whole-benchmark baselines average to (57.5 + 62.5 + 54.4)/3 = 58.1333%. These derived averages expose different conditions/reporting; they do not reconcile the discrepancy. [C] Usability findings indicate small perceived impact for the sampled users and pages, with close rendered similarity. They do not establish perfect accessibility or functionality across every application. The loading table contains larger delays than the narrative's illustrative claim. Generation is roughly three minutes per page, whereas client restoration is roughly 52 milliseconds; calling both simply 'low overhead' obscures this deployment distinction. [A/D] ## 10. Figure-by-Figure Interpretation ### Figure 1 — Parse-then-interpret mechanism, p. 2 A diagram shows dense webpage input → Agent Parse → simplified content → Agent Interpret. Attacker-prompt guidance enters interpretation, with a feedback-style arrow suggesting guidance around that stage. The dense input is labeled averaged 332k tokens; reduced content can be about 1k tokens. These are diagram labels, not a reported universal compression ratio. No axes or statistical uncertainty apply. It supports the two dependency points used by WebCloak. [A/B] ### Figure 2 — Benchmark construction, p. 5 Panel (a) displays the five content categories and challenges from dynamic content, A/B testing, and personalization. Panel (b) flows from selection of 50 websites through offline snapshots to preprocessing of 237 pages, then annotation with automated asset statistics and manual verification. Panel (c) lists five categories, 50 websites, 237 pages, 10,895 images, and 332,079 mean tokens. A lower strip groups reproducibility, image-specific ground truth, and systematic evaluation contributions. This is a pipeline, not a statistical plot; the token count is an average per page. [A/B] ### Figure 3 — Thirty-two screening variants, p. 6 Horizontal stacked bars list scraper variants vertically and sum recall across five websites horizontally, reaching up to 500%. Website categories use different fills; agent names are blue for L2S, green for LNC, and red for LWA. The x-axis total is a sum of five percentages, not recall above 100% on a single page. Individual segment labels are percentages. High totals for leading tools contrast with zero/low bars for several agents. Small segment labels are not all confidently transcribed; Table 1 and prose provide the main numerical findings. No error bars or run variability are shown. [B] ### Figure 4 — Two-layer architecture, p. 8 An original page feeds Dynamic Structural Obfuscation and Optimized Semantic Labyrinth, which combine into a WebCloak page. The plus/combination symbol communicates complementary protection. Actual construction order is semantic insertion first, structural transformation second according to §6.3. The figure is conceptual and does not specify an API, timing budget, or execution schedule. [A/B] ### Figure 5 — Structural transformation and restoration, p. 8 The diagram contrasts standard image markup with nonstandard randomized representation. A central flow labels CSPRNG, obfuscation, honeypot, and keep-as-is operations. A lower user-side path connects original and protected pages that look identical, with post-loading de-obfuscation and a de-obfuscator, and identifies Shadow DOM in the resulting representation. The exact code strings are examples; no particular random identifier is a required system constant. The key separation is visible rendering versus the structural cues encountered by automation. [A/B] ### Figure 6 — Semantic-defense optimization, p. 9 The left portion initializes pre/intra/post injection points and illustrates repeated Defend-LLM/Attack-LLM interaction, simplification, and final selection. The right portion contrasts original image markup with added hidden warnings and altered descriptive attributes. Arrows represent candidate construction, attack evaluation, and iterative refinement. There are no quantitative axes. Extracted diagram text contains duplicated content, notation corruption, and an apparent editorial comment; those are not used as method claims. The visible figure and §6.2 support the interpretation. [A/B] ### Figure 7 — Semantic-layer removal stress test, p. 12 The x-axis is percentage of defensive prompts removed, 0–100%; the y-axis is recall, 0–100%. Blue circles represent Crawl4AI and orange squares Browser-Use. Both stay low over earlier removal levels and rise sharply near complete removal. Reported 90%-removal values are 30.5% and 21.2%; final visible labels at 100% removal are 97.1% and 85.0%. Other visible annotations include 12.8%, 11.8%, and 20.1%, but not all are assigned to exact removal positions here because small-label association is less certain. No error bars appear. This tests Part 2 alone, not combined protection. [A/B] ### Figure 8 — User ratings and disagreement, p. 13 Five paired bar groups correspond to Q1–Q5. Blue bars use the left axis, average rating on a 1–7 scale, lower better. Orange bars use the right axis, disagreement percentage, higher better, because statements describe negative effects. Exact means are 1.67, 1.42, 1.55, 1.77, 1.55; percentages are 90.00%, 99.40%, 89.70%, 89.10%, 91.40%. A disagreement threshold of ≤3.0 appears in the caption. The percentage denominator is unclear because percentages do not correspond to simple single-response counts out of 35. No error bars or significance markings appear. [A/B/D] ### Figure 9 — HTML token distribution, p. 19 A histogram places token count on the horizontal axis with a ×10^6 multiplier and webpage count vertically, approximately 0–25. The horizontal display reaches about 1.6 million tokens. Many pages cluster toward the lower end, with a long tail and occasional very large pages. The caption says most exceed 200,000 tokens and argues direct full-HTML LLM processing is impractical. Exact bin boundaries, tokenization method, and per-bin counts are not supplied, so no independent median or percentile is calculated. This supports large-input motivation without proving every current model incapable of reading each page. [A/B/D] ## 11. Table-by-Table Interpretation ### Table 1 — Paradigm screening, p. 6 Rows L2S/LNC/LWA contain 19/5/8 variants, with 19/4/7 runnable. The No.1 recall column is 84.2/98.0/99.3%; the separate minimal viable recall (MVR) column is 73.7/76.0/25.0%. Its note defines MVR as the ratio of crawlers extracting at least one image URL on each website. Prose labels the top-performing numbers as MVR, conflicting with the column distinction. Diagram / Architecture Interpretation Figures 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6 are the architecture and workflow diagrams; their individual coverage appears above. Together they describe two interacting data paths. The normal scraping path takes source/rendered page structure, reduces it using parsers, and sends selected information to an LLM that decides what to extract. L2S instead has an LLM generate code whose assumptions determine which structures are found. [A] The protected path starts with original page context. A generation-time optimization loop creates contextual pre/intra/post cues. Those cues and asset elements are then structurally transformed. The delivered page contains nonstandard structure plus restoration code. In the human path, JavaScript reconstructs the intended visual assets. In the agent path, standard parsing may miss true assets or follow honeypots; surviving contextual text can redirect interpretation. [A/D] The optimizer's feedback is an Attack-LLM extraction result returned to the Defend LLM for refinement. That loop is a preparation procedure rather than a required fresh attack simulation during every human page load. The paper distinguishes expensive generation from lightweight restoration. It does not specify production interfaces, caching invalidation, encryption parameters, or a complete browser observability boundary. [A/D] ## 13. Equations and Mathematical Concepts **E1 — Recall, p. 10, §7.1:** `R = |C_extract ∩ C_target| / |C_target|`. `C_extract` is the extracted-item set, `C_target` the ground-truth target set, intersection selects correctly retrieved targets, and vertical bars denote set cardinality. Recall measures how much of the desired content was retrieved. Lower recall favors defense. Multiplying the fraction by 100 expresses a percentage. A zero-target convention is not supplied. [A] Precision is verbally defined as the proportion of extracted items that are correct targets. Its corresponding explanatory identity is `P = |C_extract ∩ C_target| / |C_extract|`; this is a direct formalization of the supplied definition, not a separately numbered author equation. If nothing is extracted, the denominator is zero. Tables report 0.0 precision in blocked conditions, but the implementation convention is not explained. Zero precision could also accompany extraction of incorrect honeypots, so it should not automatically be read as zero output items. [A/D] On p. 6, recall is described instead as correctly extracted URLs among all extractions, which corresponds to precision under §7.1. This is a definition inconsistency. The p. 10 explicit target-denominator formula is the clearest available recall definition; the p. 6 wording remains flagged rather than silently corrected. [A] `D_LLM` and `A_LLM` denote defense-generation and attack-simulation models. `p_pre`, `p_intra`, and `p_post` are text snippets for three insertion zones. `branchfactor` denotes candidate-set generation breadth; `top_k` denotes retained strategies; depth denotes iterative refinement level. Values are unspecified. `t_part1`, `t_part2`, and `t_full` denote generation times, not objective functions. [A; pp. 9, 13] No numbered optimization loss, theorem, proof, or executable pseudocode is supplied. The 'optimization' is scored candidate search and refinement using extraction outcomes. Diagram notation for full DOM and simplified text/Markdown is explanatory; corrupt extracted superscripts are not promoted into equations. ## 14. Interpretation and Discussion **Introductory RQ1:** The screening, strong representative results, and effort study support the claim that tested LLM-assisted systems can lower the barrier to image extraction. They do not quantify real-world unauthorized scraping prevalence or total economic harm. **RQ2:** The paper identifies structural preprocessing and semantic interpretation as dependencies. The defense's observed effects are consistent with this explanation, although layer-specific traces and broader causal measurements would strengthen it. **RQ3:** The combined defense is effective under the tested threat model and mostly well-rated by sampled users, with significant generation costs and some adaptive residual extraction. [A/D] For the user's research question, the architecture adds a useful mechanism-level explanation: agents consume untrusted page content through parsers, descriptions, and browser representations, and can act on the model's resulting interpretation. Hidden text can survive simplification and compete with extraction instructions. Structural transformations can also cause failures before the model receives useful evidence. These are different mechanisms: prompt susceptibility is semantic, while missed assets may be parser failure. Treating both as one generic 'LLM vulnerability' would obscure the findings. [D; pp. 7–9] The paper's cited discussion says some prior agents execute harmful instructions they would refuse in chat, and reference [15] has the user's research-question title. Those are reported literature positions, not this paper's controlled standalone comparison. The actual supplied experiment is agents versus protected/unprotected pages, not agents versus isolated LLMs. Thus comparative vulnerability magnitude remains UNKNOWN from this work. Contributions and Novelty **Conceptual:** A website-owner-centered agent-as-attacker framing, separating deliberate malicious use from compromise of an otherwise legitimate agent. **Empirical:** A 32-variant screening, three-paradigm detailed comparison, effort observations, and identified operational dependencies. **Dataset/benchmark:** Offline image-rich pages with main-content ground truth and repeatable extraction tasks. **System/methodological:** Two complementary layers combining dynamic representation changes with optimized hidden contextual cues. **Experimental:** Baseline, instruction, backend, adaptation, removal, cross-environment, usability, and overhead studies. [A; pp. 2–14] No new theorem, standalone model architecture, or model-training algorithm is claimed. The semantic search adapts an iterative adversarial-generation approach cited by the paper. The authors claim first systematic characterization and benchmark priority; those remain unverified author claims in closed-document mode. Appendix D recognizes a dataset, tool, and useful advance, but questions the extra advantage over standard defenses, absence of social media, and novelty of defensive prompt injection. Appendix E argues that rendered-DOM resilience and adaptive robustness supply the extra advantage. A balanced reading locates novelty primarily in the combined system, threat characterization, benchmark, and dynamic defense evaluation rather than claiming defensive prompt injection itself is new. The latter assessment is analyst interpretation informed by the included review. [A/D; p. 20] ## 16. Limitations ### Authors' stated limitations JavaScript is required for visual restoration; disabling it can break the intended display. The cited under-0.2% prevalence claim is author-reported background, not verified current prevalence. A determined expert could reverse-engineer a single randomized session, although the authors argue scaling this is expensive. Large-scale evidence is image-centric; audio/text protection is tested on a smaller supplementary set, and a comprehensive multimodal benchmark is needed. Approximately three-minute semantic generation may challenge rapidly changing sites such as social media. Protection is deliberately scoped to novice/intermediate scalable misuse rather than all expert attacks. [A; pp. 4, 13–14] ### Additional evidence-based analyst observations The supplied work has inconsistent metrics/aggregates and incomplete experimental settings. Two small human studies lack uncertainty reporting. The 27-page comparison subset is selected for vulnerability and cannot estimate average production-site performance. Offline preprocessing can alter dynamic behavior even when visual appearance is preserved. Exact randomization, resource encoding, restoration code, and generation hyperparameters are absent. Browser and backend tests cover selected systems, not all possible models or extraction routes. Similar visuals do not by themselves establish assistive-technology compatibility, identical semantics, or full interaction fidelity. These are analyst observations, not author admissions. [D] ## 17. Threats to Validity **Internal validity [D]:** Layer effects are supported by isolated adaptation/removal studies, but a complete factorial ablation across the full benchmark is absent. Unresolved baseline differences and recall wording make some cross-experiment comparisons uncertain. Repetition counts and stochastic variability are not reported. **Construct validity [D]:** URL extraction is used as the main success proxy. It measures retrieval of annotated addresses, not necessarily successful downloads, downstream misuse, or economic loss. Main-content annotation excludes decorative and small assets; a broader extraction objective could yield different judgments. High visual similarity and low negative ratings are narrower than perfect user transparency. **External/ecological validity [D]:** Fifty source sites and five categories improve diversity, but local frozen pages omit live change, authentication, request traffic, and many interactive conditions. Social media is explicitly identified as absent in the meta-review. Audio/text has only five pages per modality. Five usability pages and 35 participants cannot establish all-platform experience. **Statistical conclusion validity [D]:** No standard errors, confidence intervals, significance tests, or variability across repeated model calls are shown. A reported 0.0% is an observed outcome at available precision, not a statistical guarantee. User-study disagreement percentages need an explicit response denominator. Weighted versus unweighted category and page aggregation is often unclear. **Reproducibility [D]:** Snapshots, standardized tasks, platforms, and annotation procedures help, and artifact badges are visible. Nevertheless the supplied package lacks code, dataset files, detailed versioning, seeds, optimization values, and logs. Reproducibility is described and partially supported, not independently demonstrated by this analysis. ## 18. Future Work and Open Questions **A. Explicit author directions:** Build a comprehensive multimodal benchmark to substantiate broader asset protection; devote more effort to trustworthy and resilient AI agents. The authors also suggest batch transformation and caching as practical ways to manage generation overhead for low-update-frequency content. Their dynamic-image update simulation is preliminary rather than a fully reported future deployment solution. [A; pp. 13–14] **B. Analyst-derived open questions:** What happens with continuously changing pages or social-media interaction? How does performance vary across repeated model calls and new tool releases? Can the same model be compared directly in standalone and agent configurations with matched malicious content? What fraction of failures comes from parsing versus semantic redirection? Does page protection preserve accessibility semantics and all user interactions? How much operator time and cost is required for adaptive bypass at scale? Which aggregation rules resolve the inconsistent means? Can audio/text findings replicate on a larger benchmark? These are remaining questions, not additional author experiments or demonstrated failures. [D] ## 19. Very Simple Explanation — Explain Like I'm 15 Imagine asking an AI to collect all the useful pictures from a website. Some AI tools write a program to do it; others read a simplified page; others control a browser. The researchers found that many such tools work, and using them can save people a lot of coding effort. That is useful for legitimate tasks, but it also makes unauthorized copying easier. WebCloak changes how a page is represented without intentionally changing what a person sees. One layer replaces familiar image labels and resource clues with changing, unusual ones. A small browser script still displays the pictures for people. Another layer adds hidden text designed to distract or mislead the AI reading the page. The important idea is that the computer's simplified map of the page can differ from the page a human sees. The defense stopped extraction in many ordinary tests. More informed attackers sometimes recovered a small amount, and the researchers do not claim protection against every expert method. There are also contradictory numbers in the paper, and the tests mostly use saved pages rather than running websites. Preparing a protected page takes about three minutes on average; displaying it adds about 52 milliseconds of restoration work, although some loading measures show larger effects. For the question about why web agents might be more vulnerable than standalone chat models, this paper suggests an extra source of weakness: an agent must trust enough information from webpage software and content to do its job. That creates opportunities to confuse its parser or influence its model. But this study never directly tests the same model alone against the same model acting as a web agent, so it cannot tell us the size of that difference. ## Completeness Audit Coverage is assessed against the supplied inventory, not response length. claims.statement: LLMCrawlBench comprises 237 pages from 50 high-traffic websites in five categories, with 10,895 image assets and reported average HTML length of 332,079 tokens.
The initial screening tests 32 variants—19 L2S, five LNC, and eight LWA—on five pages, one per category; the paper reports 84.4% can extract multiple correct images.
The authors identify a parse-then-interpret dependency for LNC/LWA systems and distinguish L2S code-generated parsing; predictable structural assumptions motivate the defense.
WebCloak combines session-randomized structural transformation with optimized hidden semantic cues; semantic injection precedes structural obfuscation during preparation.
On a selected 27-page high-vulnerability comparison subset, original recalls are 93.1%, 95.3%, and 77.7% for Gemini, Crawl4AI, and Browser-Use; full WebCloak reports 0.0% for each.
The Table 5 baseline mean is (93.1 + 95.3 + 77.7)/3 = 88.7%; reduction to zero is 88.7 percentage points and 100% relative reduction within that selected-subset experiment.
Under adaptive L2S attempts, static target obfuscation rises to 52.3% recall while WebCloak Part 1 rises only to 0.13%; these are structural-layer isolation results.

The full defense has nonzero residual recall in modeled knowledgeable attacks: Table 10 reports 0.20% L2S and 1.58% Crawl4AI; multi-turn knowledgeable L2S reaches 0.30% with two to three refinement turns.
With 90% of defensive prompts removed from Part 2-only protection, recall remains 21.2% for Browser-Use and 30.5% for Crawl4AI; this is not a full-defense result.
Audio/text generalization uses ten supplementary evaluation pages, five per modality; this smaller study cannot establish universal multimodal protection.
Table 15 reports average protected-page generation time of 179.7 seconds and client restoration time of 0.052 seconds; server preparation and client execution are materially different costs.
Protection is scoped to novice-to-intermediate operators prioritizing scalability and low cost, excluding expensive repeated manual repair and bespoke expert circumvention.
The supplied results contain unresolved discrepancies, including Table 8's all-zero protected backend entries versus nearby prose reporting 2.9% DeepSeek-V3 residual recall.
The authors acknowledge JavaScript dependence, possible expert reverse engineering, and the image-centric limits of large-scale evaluation.

For the requested research question, this work supplies mechanism-level relevance: agent parsing and webpage interpretation expose structural dependencies and untrusted contextual influence. It does not directly measure vulnerability relative to matched standalone LLMs.
The included meta-review questions comparative advantage, social-media coverage, and novelty of defensive prompt injection; these concerns qualify the authors' novelty and generalization claims.

limitations: All 20 pages were assessed textually; only 17 supplied page images were visually inspected.
The source hash and accessibility metadata were supplied and were not independently verified.
No tools, browsing, external research, OCR, replication, or artifact inspection was performed.
Dense Figure 3 segments and uncertain Figure 6 extraction notation were compressed or flagged.
Unresolved reporting conflicts affect recalls, MVR terminology, text aggregates, backend robustness, loading delays, token averages, site examples, and cross-references.
Exact tool versions, random seeds, repetition counts, optimization hyperparameters, statistical uncertainty, and several aggregation denominators are absent.
No controlled comparison of web agents with matched standalone LLMs is supplied; research relevance is analyst inference.
Underlying benchmark, supplementary datasets, implementation, and logs were not provided.

research.title: WebCloak: Characterizing and Mitigating Threats from LLM-Driven Web Agents as Intelligent Scrapers
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, analyst inference: the paper shows how webpage preprocessing and LLM interpretation create agent-specific dependencies and opportunities for hidden contextual redirection. This is relevant to explaining additional attack surfaces in web-connected systems. It studies agent-as-attacker scraping and defensive interference, however, and does not directly compare matched web agents with standalone LLMs. Comparative vulnerability magnitude is UNKNOWN from the supplied work.
research.attack_surface: Page HTML/DOM, conventional image tags and source attributes, parser simplification and Markdown conversion, hidden pre/post elements and image alt text, rendered browser representations, and client-side restoration. The attacker in the paper is a malicious scraper operator; the website owner uses structural and semantic interference defensively.
research.method: Construct 237 offline pages from 50 websites with 10,895 annotated images; screen 32 variants across L2S/LNC/LWA on five pages; characterize three representatives across the benchmark; evaluate dynamic structural obfuscation plus iteratively optimized semantic cues against baselines, task instructions, backends, adaptation, prompt removal, environments, usability, and overhead.
research.limitations: Novice/intermediate scalable-attacker scope; local offline snapshots; JavaScript-dependent restoration; expert reverse engineering remains possible; ten-page audio/text extension; small human studies; absent statistical uncertainty and detailed version/configuration information; unresolved numerical inconsistencies; no direct standalone-LLM comparison; underlying artifacts not supplied.
